audience.programmeDescription: WUR’s Dutch-taught Plant Sciences bachelor studies how plants function and interact with their environment, from cells and genes to crops and agroecosystems. It combines biological research with applications to food production, health, renewable resources and environmental resilience.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR programme connects biological mechanisms with ecology, farming and soil-environment study. The second emphasises molecular, laboratory and computational methods; the third focuses on sustainable farming and resource-policy decisions. WUR provides substantially more plant physiology, crop recognition, breeding, pest management and specialist greenhouse/field research. Its 18-credit thesis is required; UCR’s optional independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 credits.

componentNotes.bpw-intro: An 8-credit introduction with disciplinary case studies, field/lab activity and academic development. The written tests and group report each require a passing mark; the personal development plan and information-literacy work must also pass. General, laboratory and fieldwork safety are additional zero-credit requirements.
componentNotes.bpw-crop-recognition: A separate 2-credit course in identifying crop species and products. Attendance, workbook/excursion and longitudinal assignments must be completed, and the recognition test must pass; this is distinct from the introductory course.
componentNotes.bpw-choice: The 3-credit choice depends on prior mathematics: this example takes Mathematics Applied: Introduction for Mathematics A preparation. Students with Mathematics B take Statistics 1. Statistics 2 assumes active school statistics or Statistics 1.
componentNotes.bpw-practice: Includes ecological field data, a group-designed greenhouse experiment, presentations, company/institution visits and interviews with three plant-science professionals. Reflection must pass; presentations require a sufficient combined result and minimum marks for their components.
componentNotes.bpw-integrated-research: A 12-credit integrated research course. Students conduct a project in pairs, write an individual scientific paper, and work across molecular-to-agroecosystem perspectives on a resilience case. The paper and group case each require a passing mark; individual reflection must also pass.
componentNotes.bpw-thesis: Required 18-credit individual plant-science research project: proposal, experiments, data analysis, written report, oral presentation, discussion and reflection/future study plan. Entry requires coordinator permission and at least 102 prescribed credits, including all first-year credits. This example completes all 132 prescribed taught credits before the thesis; permission remains a requirement.
componentNotes.bpw-electives: Thirty open credits remain for a minor and/or individual electives. Seagriculture, Experimental Plant Sciences and Resilient Crops are optional minors, not additional compulsory specialisations; no particular minor is assumed.
componentNotes.bpw-genetics: The UCR relationship is partial: shared inheritance, variation, gene regulation and DNA technologies are studied in a human-disease context. WUR also develops Mendelian mapping, population and evolutionary genetics and complex traits.
componentNotes.bpw-evolution: UCR studies selection, genetic variation, genomics and phylogeny across organisms. WUR focuses on plant evolution, crop domestication, crop wild relatives and genetic resources.
componentNotes.bpw-systems: The UCR relationship concerns numerical differential-equation and equation-system methods. WUR also teaches ecological model formulation, calibration/evaluation and spatial, crop and soil simulation cases.
componentNotes.bpw-soil-plant: UCR contributes soil properties and field/laboratory measurement, alongside aquifer study. WUR adds a dedicated focus on roots, the rhizosphere and plant water/nutrient uptake.

concepts: Investigate biological and ecological mechanisms relevant to plants and sustainable agricultural systems. selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Living with Water
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, using Zeeland as a central case. Flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinisation, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, then apply these ideas through site-based inquiry and a project on delta adaptation.
